The official definition covers both teaching-focused and teaching-research combined positions. It can be understood in three work dimensions: course design and materials; lecturing, discussion and lab / project supervision; and evaluation, records and academic service. Research-combined positions may also supervise research, publish outputs and apply for funding, so the whole occupation cannot be limited to the cycle of a single course. The three divisions are editorial synthesis, not a distribution of separate positions.
Turn course objectives and prerequisites into a syllabus, lecture notes, assignments and lab arrangements, and write out the assessment method and the credit and contact hour scope.

Teach topics such as programming, data structures and software design to undergraduate or graduate students, lead classroom discussion and supervise labs and projects.

Prepare examples and exercises before class → teach concepts and demonstrate → organize classroom discussion and questions → supervise labs or projects → office hours and individual guidance → record student participation and questions

Evaluation and records → academic advising and committee service; research-combined positions may also conduct research, supervise graduate students, publish outputs or apply for funding, checked against job duties.

The six teaching checks are editorial suggestions; among the O*NET26 tasks there are 16 Core and 10 Supplemental, with course materials / exams both 90, lecturing 87, grading 85, records 80, and research supervision 81 / research publication 78 as Supplemental, which are not present in every position or their task frequency.
Judgment one: whether the course objectives and prerequisites are explained clearly

Write course objectives, prerequisites and credits and contact hours into a checkable checklist; confirm content connecting to prerequisite courses and overlapping with later courses with the course lead first, and do not compress or expand content on impression.
Judgment two: whether the lecture notes and examples are correct and consistent with the syllabus

Check definitions, code examples, complexity and run results in the lecture notes one by one; confirm the examples match the assessment scope this time, and do not take unverified generated content straight into the classroom.
Judgment three: whether the assignment and lab conditions are executable

Confirm that students can complete assignments and labs in the given environment and time, and write out the inputs, available libraries and versions, submission format and grading points; do not use environments or data students cannot obtain.
Judgment four: whether the grading criteria are consistent and explicable

Write the grading points and marks before grading, and handle similar errors by the same standard; keep the basis for judgment on borderline answers and be able to restate to the student why marks were deducted.
Judgment five: whether grade and attendance records are complete and traceable

Record attendance, assignments and exam results as required by the institution, and corrections must leave traces; handle student personal information and grades according to institutional systems, and do not export or copy them privately.
Judgment six: whether course revisions leave a basis

Propose revisions based on student feedback, grade distribution and disciplinary change, write out the reasons and scope of impact, and submit them through the course approval process, without directly overwriting the published syllabus.

When choosing a direction, first look at what reviewable evidence you can present: the teaching and curriculum direction looks at course materials and student feedback, the research and student supervision direction looks at papers, projects and supervision records, and the education management and technical support direction looks at organizational coordination or system support records; no single ranking is given by income or personality.

The adjacent directions are taken from the slugs registered in this evidence route (computer and information systems managers, management consultants, computer systems analysts, computer and information research scientists, computer programmers) and from teaching support occupations present in the frozen index (instructional coordinators); the comparison is based on O*NET occupational detail profiles and adjacent occupation sections.

This table compares postsecondary computer science teachers with six adjacent directions on the same dimensions: core work and outputs, the key difference from teaching responsibility, and what preparation background suits it better; tasks and tools may overlap, but course responsibility, grade authority and academic record responsibility do not transfer with the job title.

Key difference: managers are responsible for department resources and delivery, not for the content taught in a specific course or student grades; this occupation is responsible for courses and evaluation and usually does not hold department budget and personnel decision authority.

What suits whom better: if you would rather coordinate resources, work across teams and manage service levels, and already have delivery management experience, that direction may be worth considering; if you would rather stay with students and course content over the long term, staying in the teaching direction is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: coordinate the personnel, budget, projects and service levels of an information technology department, producing department plans, budgets and delivery results.
Computer and information systems managers

Key difference: analysts face business and systems and their deliverables are requirements and solutions; this occupation faces students and courses and its deliverables are lecture notes, assignments, grades and grade records.

What suits whom better: if you would rather do requirements research and solution design and repeatedly clarify goals with business parties, that direction may be worth considering; if you would rather organize knowledge into a course and grade assignments one by one, staying in the teaching direction is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: turn business requirements into system solutions and specifications, producing requirement documents, processes and solution recommendations.
Computer systems analysts

Key difference: research scientists use research innovation as the main evaluation standard; even when this occupation carries research tasks, teaching and course responsibility cannot be omitted, and grade record responsibility does not transfer because of research output.

What suits whom better: if you would rather do experiments and papers over the long term with research output as the main evaluation line, that direction may be worth considering; if you are willing to put part of your energy steadily into courses and student supervision, a teaching-research combined position is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: conduct algorithm and model research and publish results, producing papers, experimental designs and reproducible results.
Computer and information research scientists

Key difference: programmers are responsible for code correctness and maintainability; this occupation is responsible for course content, student evaluation and grade records, and coding ability is teaching material rather than the deliverable itself.

What suits whom better: if you would rather keep writing code and delivering software, that direction may be worth considering; if you would rather explain and evaluate other people's learning process, staying in the teaching direction is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: write, modify and test code and scripts according to specifications, producing runnable and maintainable programs and documentation.
Computer programmers

Key difference: support specialists are mainly measured by how quickly user problems are resolved; this occupation is mainly measured by course delivery and student evaluation, and students are not ticket objects.

What suits whom better: if you would rather do troubleshooting and user support and have a service mindset, that direction may be worth considering; if you would rather face long-term learning processes and evaluation work, staying in the teaching direction is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: provide end users with account, device and software support, producing problem handling results and support records.
Computer support specialists

Key difference: instructional coordinators are responsible for the curriculum system and teaching quality processes; this occupation is responsible for the teaching, grading and grade records of specific courses, and the two draw authority from different sources.

What suits whom better: if you would rather do cross-department coordination, curriculum standards and teacher development work, that direction may be worth considering; if you would rather teach in person and evaluate students, a teaching position is more suitable.
Core work and outputs: coordinate courses, teacher training and teaching quality management, producing course schedules, training plans and quality reports.
Instructional coordinators

If you value long-term classroom interaction and the student growth process more, the teaching direction is the main line; if you value system solutions, research or department coordination more, you need to add the corresponding evidence before considering a shift, and this table does not constitute a hiring or promotion promise.

The five steps below are the editorial process suggestion given on this page (not a mandatory process prescribed by a source): first clarify the learning objectives and the boundary of usable evidence, then have tools generate drafts, then check them manually, then record the changes, and finally specify who is responsible for grades and academic judgments.

First determine the learning objectives of this course task, the materials that may be used and the scope of data that must not be input externally; clarify what content tools may take part in and what must be completed independently by the teacher.

Editorial suggestion: in environments the institution permits and that have been validated, trial materials, code and feedback; check versions, citations, criteria and data handling, and do not automatically enter real courses or grades.

Check facts, code run results, difficulty and prerequisite fit, citations and copyright item by item; discard or rewrite any content that fails the check in full, and do not carry doubts into the classroom and grading stages.

Record which content was generated by tools and which was modified by the teacher, and the reasons for modification; records involving grades, attendance and academic integrity are kept according to institutional systems.

Grade determination, grade correction, academic integrity determination and appeal handling are completed by authorized teachers or institutional processes; tools do not carry grade responsibility and do not constitute a formal evaluation of the student.

Lecture notes and problems entering the classroom and exams directly mean errors will be taken by students as the standard answer; erroneous examples may also affect the prerequisite foundation of later courses.

Before release, check definitions, code run results and citation sources item by item; replace unverifiable material with verified material or mark it as pending confirmation, and do not publish generated content directly.

Assignments, grades, contact information and identity information are protected materials, and inputting them into external services may violate institutional systems and applicable jurisdiction requirements.

Confirm the permitted scope and tools according to institutional systems, remove identifiable information, and use institution-approved channels; when unsure, ask the data protection or academic affairs department first and do not upload on your own initiative.
Being unable to state which tool, which version and which prompts were used makes it hard to check the content source and modification process in a dispute.

Record the tool name and version, generation time and key modifications; keep the teacher's confirmation record for the final published version so the content can be traced to a specific responsible person.
The difficulty distribution of generated problems and examples may deviate from the course positioning, and students either cannot complete them or fail to meet the assessment objectives.

entries.answer: This occupation has course teaching and student evaluation as its core responsibility: computer and information systems managers focus on department resource and delivery coordination; computer systems analysts focus on translating business requirements into system solutions; computer and information research scientists focus on algorithm and model research; computer programmers focus on code delivery; computer support specialists focus on user and device support. entries.question: What education is needed to become a postsecondary computer science teacher?

entries.answer: The O*NET certification search lists candidate certification examples (such as Microsoft Certified Trainer, Certified Professional Instructor, Internet Business Associate and others), which can serve as supplementary capability material but are not a postsecondary teaching threshold. In the United States, postsecondary teaching and appointment conditions are set by institutions; for Mainland China, no national unified public teaching qualification conditions were obtained, so the target institution and competent authority rules must be checked.
entries.question: Which certificates or qualifications are needed?

entries.answer: It is feasible but teaching capability must be demonstrated: industry experience can support practical training and project courses, but institutions usually also look at course design, grading criteria and student evaluation capability. It is suggested to verify first with complete course materials and a mock lecture, or to take on one module, lab supervision or an adjunct course first and then gradually take on a full course.
entries.question: Is it feasible to switch from another industry into postsecondary computer science teaching?

entries.answer: It depends on whether you are willing to invest in teaching and evaluation work over the long term: the value of this work comes from explaining courses clearly and giving students consistent, explicable evaluation of their assignments and exams; the cost is that preparation, grading and answering questions continue to take time (the work context shows 57% working more than 40 hours per week). This page provides task and evidence boundaries and does not constitute personal career advice.
